title: We're Not Afraid to Die… if We Can Be Together (Hornbill)
tagline: A family’s voyage in Wavewalker, a storm in the southern ocean, and the children whose courage steadies their father.

overview.intro: Based on a real voyage, this account turns a survival story into a study of composure. A family sails round the world, meets a storm that floods and capsizes their boat, and holds together partly through seamanship and partly through the words of two children. The unit follows the sequence of the voyage, the mechanics of the damage and the repair, and the moment the title’s sentence is spoken — and asks why that sentence, rather than the pumps and the canvas, is what the narrator builds the story around.

learningOutcomes: Sequence the events of the voyage and the storm.
Explain the technical difficulties: flooding, failed pumps, capsizing and repair.
Account for the significance of the children’s reactions.
Identify how the narrative builds tension through detail and pacing.
Answer extract and long questions on the account with evidence.

blocks.text: The narrative is in the first person and begins with the ambition that prompted it: a family deciding to prove that their dream of sailing the world could be done. They set out from Plymouth in Wavewalker with a plan of roughly two years and take on crew for the hardest stretch, the southern ocean, where the great westerly winds run unobstructed round the globe. The plan is described with the confidence of preparation — provisions, route, extra hands — which the storm will then test, and the account is careful to establish that this was not recklessness but an expedition that had been thought through.

The early passage of the voyage is written to show competence: the family handles the boat, the children are at home at sea, and the crew are professionals. That matters for the story’s argument, because the disaster that follows is not the result of error. The account gives the weather rather than the crew as the antagonist, and by establishing that everyone knew what they were doing, it makes the later tension about endurance rather than about blame.

items: The family sails from Plymouth with a plan of about two years.
They take on crew for the southern ocean passage.
The early sections establish competence and routine at sea.
The antagonist is weather, not inexperience.
Preparation is described fully before it is tested.

learn.title: The storm: damage, flooding and capsizing

blocks.text: The crisis arrives as a sequence rather than as a single blow. Heavy seas strike the boat, water comes in, and the vessel is damaged in ways that compound: leaks spread, the pumps fail or clog with debris, and the crew must bail while keeping the boat under control. The narrator is injured, and his wife and the crew take on work well beyond the plan. The description is technical in the best sense — the reader is told what broke, what was tried and what failed — because each technical detail raises the stakes: a failed pump means the difference between a repairable boat and a sinking one.

The boat capsizes and rights itself, an event the account handles with restraint, and from that point the story is about whether the damaged hull can be kept afloat long enough to reach land. The narrative pacing is worth studying: paragraphs of action are followed by short factual statements of depth, distance and time, which has the effect of slowing the reader down at precisely the moments when the family has no time at all. Attention is then redirected to the children, whose behaviour is reported rather than dramatised — they are frightened, they are sick, and yet they do not add to the burden — and that redirection prepares the emotional centre of the piece.

Repairs must hold for days, not hours

learn.title: The sentence the title comes from

blocks.text: At the point of greatest strain the narrator turns to his children and finds them composed rather than hysterical, and it is Jonathan who says that they are not afraid to die if they can all be together. The line is doing several things at once. It states the children’s courage, it converts the disaster from a technical problem into a question of what matters, and it supplies the father with resolve at the moment when resolve is the only remaining resource. The account gives it the title because the whole narrative bends toward it: every preceding paragraph of preparation and every technical detail of damage is arranged so that this sentence can arrive as the story’s conclusion rather than as an aside.

The line also resolves the narrative’s tension in a specific way. The family cannot repair the sea; they can only endure it and steer. What the sentence supplies is the reason endurance is possible, and the story’s interest lies in that: the account is not about a boat that was saved by seamanship alone but about a family whose coherence was the condition of its survival. Answers that reduce the story to a list of damages miss the point the title insists on.

items.text: Jonathan’s sentence at the height of the storm.
items.note: The emotional centre: courage stated by a child rather than narrated by an adult.

items.text: The failed pumps and the hand-bailing.
items.note: Technical detail that raises the stakes without commentary.

blocks.text: The narrative technique is worth naming for examination purposes. It uses a first-person retrospective voice, so every event is already known to be survived, which allows the narrator to alternate between immediacy and reflection: he can give the action in short present-tense-feeling sentences and then step back to explain what a repair meant. Information is released in increments — first the weather, then the leak, then the pump, then the injury — so that the reader’s understanding deteriorates in step with the boat’s condition.

The second technique is contrast. Calm domestic details — the children asleep, the plan, the provisions — are set against the storm, and the children’s composure is set against the adults’ exertion. This is why the piece survives being retold: its tension comes from arrangement rather than from adjectives. For answers, quote one technical detail and one domestic detail in any paragraph about tension, and state what each contributes.

blocks.caption: Techniques and their effects

Danger becomes concrete rather than dramatic
What is at stake is named without stating it
Releases tension into feeling at the right moment

questions.answer: Demonstrates that their composure gave the adults resolve at the point of greatest strain
questions.explanation: Their calm is reported at the moment the narrator most needs it, and it converts the disaster into a question of what matters.

questions.explanation: The vessel’s name is given at the start of the account and returns whenever its condition is described.

questions.prompt: Give four technical details of the crisis described in the account.
questions.answer: Four details are: heavy seas strike the boat and water enters the hull; the pumps fail or clog with debris so that bailing has to be done by hand; the narrator is injured at a moment when his skill is most needed; and the boat capsizes and rights itself, leaving the hull more badly damaged than before. Steering for the nearest refuge rather than attempting the original destination is also accepted.
questions.explanation: The answer must be technical and sequential, not a general statement that the storm was severe.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator give Jonathan’s sentence the title of the story?
questions.answer: The sentence — that they are not afraid to die if they can all be together — arrives at the point where the technical problem can no longer be solved, only endured, and it supplies what endurance requires: a reason. It also states the children’s courage in their own voice rather than in the narrator’s description, which gives it an authority an adult reflection would not have, and it turns the account from a record of damages into a statement about what holds a family together under stress. Structurally, the whole narrative bends toward the line: the preparation, the failed pumps, the capsize and the injuries are arranged so that the sentence can serve as the conclusion rather than as an aside. Finally, it answers the reader’s question about the children — they are frightened and sick, and yet they do not add to the burden — by showing that their composure is not ignorance but acceptance.
questions.explanation: The answer must give the sentence’s functions — supplying resolve, stating courage in the children’s voice, and organising the narrative — rather than paraphrasing it.

questions.prompt: How does the author build tension in this account? Answer with evidence.
questions.answer: Tension is built through structure and information control rather than through dramatic adjectives. The first device is incremental disclosure: the reader learns about the weather, then the leak, then the failure of the pumps, then the injury and finally the capsize, so that understanding of the danger deteriorates in step with the boat. Each item is technical rather than emotional — a pump that clogs, a hull that strains, a depth that rises — and technical specificity makes the danger concrete, because the reader can see what a failed pump actually implies for a sinking vessel. The second device is the retrospective first-person voice, which is authoritative because the narrator survived, and which allows him to alternate between immediate action and a short reflection on what a moment meant, so the pace slows exactly where the family had no time to spare. The third device is contrast: the plan, the provisions and the sleeping children are placed against the storm, which names what is at stake without ever stating it, and the children’s composure is set against the adults’ exertion to release the built-up tension into feeling. The fourth is pacing by sentence length — short factual statements of time and distance amid longer passages of action — which produces the sensation of breathlessness the subject requires. The climax is prepared rather than sprung: the children’s sentence arrives after the technical crisis has been fully established, so it reads as the story’s conclusion instead of a decorative remark. An examiner should be shown two quoted details, one technical and one domestic, with the work each does, because tension answers that generalise about excitement without citing arrangement rarely earn full marks.
questions.explanation: Full marks require at least three named techniques, two quoted details and an explanation of how the climax is prepared.

questions.prompt: Is this story about survival at sea, or about family? Discuss with reference to the whole account.
questions.answer: The case for a survival story is grounded in the narrative’s content. The account is dominated by the mechanics of the crisis: water entering the hull, pumps failing or clogging, hand-bailing, an injury to the most experienced hand, a capsize and recovery, and the steering of a damaged boat toward refuge. Its tension depends on technical specificity rather than sentiment, the narrator is a seaman whose competence is established early, and the antagonist is weather rather than any human failing — all of which belong to the tradition of maritime survival narrative, where the interest lies in whether seamanship can outrun the sea. The case for a family story rests on the architecture rather than on the events. The crew exists in the account mainly as expertise; the emotional weight is carried by the children, whose fear and sickness are reported without melodrama and whose composure is what the narrator turns to at the point of greatest strain. The sentence that becomes the title belongs to Jonathan and is about togetherness rather than rescue, and the narrator explicitly makes it the source of his resolve — that is, the survival continues because the family holds. Even the preparation sections are domestic in emphasis: this is a family’s plan, not a commercial voyage, and the stakes are stated as a shared dream rather than as cargo or schedule. The strongest reading is that the story uses the survival form to test the family claim: the technical detail establishes an objective danger so that the children’s sentence can answer it, and the two are therefore not rivals but argument and evidence. The design of the piece supports this — the title chooses the family line over any description of the storm, and the closing movement returns to people rather than to repairs. An answer that quotes both the technical sequence and the children’s moment, then judges which organises the other, will earn the marks for reasoning rather than for preference.
questions.explanation: Full marks require both readings evidenced from different parts of the account and a judgement about which organises the narrative rather than which the examiner prefers.
